S1_overlap_dependence.question: Overlapping windows (e.g. Jul01+15td and Jul01+20td) share most of their days, so their results are correlated. Did Phase 1 overstate how many independent chances it had?
S1_overlap_dependence.note: With only 20 years of data the 120 windows cannot carry more than ~20 independent pieces of information. Even crediting that, the best window does not reach significance. The original permutation test already accounted for overlap.

S2_same_year_placebo.question: The Phase-2 placebo drew random windows from anywhere in 2023-2026. Should it instead stay inside each occurrence's own year, so a 2023 trade is compared only with other 2023 trades?
S2_same_year_placebo.note: Placebo p-values here are re-computed with a different random seed, so the 'anywhere' variant will differ slightly from the original 0.36.

S3_cross_rule_tests.question: Phase 2 treated the 132 rules as independent when testing whether in-sample winners stayed winners (Spearman) and whether more than half kept their direction (binomial). The rules overlap heavily, so those p-values may be too small.
S3_cross_rule_tests.method: Shift every rule's OOS entry by the same random number of trading days (wrapping inside 2023-2026), keeping all overlaps between rules intact, and recompute both statistics 2,000 times.

S4_entry_exit.question: Do entries and exits match the frozen definitions, and does any convention change results?
S4_entry_exit.label_note: Window names such as 'Jul 1 -> Jul 22' show the TYPICAL exit date. The rule is defined in trading days, so the actual exit moves by 1-3 calendar days from year to year (the frozen file records the range).

jan_2023_entry.rule_used: Jan 2023 occurrences enter at the 2023-01-03 OPEN because the OOS file has no earlier bar (same rule Phase 1 used for Jan 2003).

S5_partial_2026.question: Were unfinished 2026 periods kept out of every statistic?
S5_partial_2026.note: Rules whose 2026 occurrence had not finished by 2026-10-02 have N = 3 instead of 4. That is correct (no partial result is used) but means late-year rules carry a little less evidence.
